catalog_quote: There is no variety of Makhuwa known to us where there is anything resembling a fully articulated system of lexical tone contrasts. Verb stems exhibit no lexical contrasts whatsoever. High tone is assigned to a particular mora or moras in the stem on the basis of the morphology in which the stem is inserted. Assignment of H tone may be to the first, second, third, or last stem mora, and in some cases to both the first and the third. ... In addition to the morphologically determined stem tone, some prefixes have a H tone associated with them in specific morphological constructions. ... Nominals (in non-focal contexts) must have at least one (underlying) H tone. In almost all dialects, this H tone must – at least in principle – be on one of the stem moras. ... The location of a H tone in the stem is largely predictable on the basis of the noun class in which the stem appears. ... It should be noted that in the dialects that do not have the contrasts in (8) (e.g. the Ruvuma dialects, Imeetto, Esaaka, Eerati), the final H pattern is impossible due to a general ban on word-final (underlying) H tones.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Makhuwa (including the Tanzanian Ruvuma dialects Ikorovere and Imitthupi and Imeetto) is a restricted tone language: H tones are placed by morphology (verbs) or largely by noun class (nouns), with H-tone doubling in many dialects that is blocked phrase-finally and on the second mora of a phrase-penult bimoraic syllable. Vowel length is contrastive. No source examined says anything about word stress; the only accessible statement on penultimate prominence is van der Wal 2009: 20 (Enahara variant): 'Makhuwa does not have automatic penultimate lenghtening as in other Bantu languages, such as Makwe and Makonde.'
new_statements.exceptions: Tone: Imitthupi shifts some H tones one mora leftward; Imeetto and the Ruvuma dialects ban word-final underlying H (so the central-dialect penult/final H contrast in class 7/8 bimoraic stems does not exist there). Nothing on stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone-doubling restrictions are stated over the phonological phrase (phrase-final, phrase-penult), not the word. The absence-of-penultimate-lengthening statement (van der Wal 2009: 20, 34) concerns the Enahara variant, not Meetto; Devos 2013 repeats it second-hand for 'Makhuwa variants' citing Kisseberth.
new_statements.identity_note: Kisseberth 2003 draws its data from the Ikorovere (Tunduru) and Imitthupi (Masasi) dialects of southern Tanzania with explicit Imeetto comparisons; Glottolog assigns Hassan 2010 (Imithupi) and Ismail 2000 (Meto) to makh1261, so these Tanzanian 'Ruvuma' varieties fall under Makhuwa-Meetto, though Ikorovere's Glottolog assignment could not be confirmed (Glottolog reference search returned no results). Kröger & Iseminger 2009 is Meetto of Cabo Delgado (Balama). van der Wal 2009 describes Makhuwa-Enahara (Ilha de Moçambique), a different variety; its no-penultimate-lengthening statement is used only as a domain note. Meinhof 1908's informant was from Newala (north of the Ruvuma) = makh1261.

In that tense the -ho- is emphasized." p. 292 (sec. 43, Past Conditional): "This tense is formed by inserting -a- between the verb and the personal prefix and changing the final -a into -ale, -ele, or -ile. new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tone language, no stress statement' (Kisseberth 2003): Woodward never mentions tone and gives no stress placement rule; what he hears as 'stress' distinguishing the -aho- past 3sg and the Past Conditional from neighbouring tenses is a morphologically conditioned prominence on the tense-prefix vowel (long aa / acute-marked a), which later work (Cheng & Kisseberth 1979; Kisseberth 2003) treats as grammatical tone on verb prefixes. It neither agrees with nor contradicts a placement reading; it adds that the earliest Ruvuma-Makua description records prominence contrasts only on tense prefixes. Also confirms, via the vowel note, contrastive vowel length without any…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general word-stress placement rule is given anywhere in the grammar. The phonology section (alphabet, p. 270-272) notes only that vowels are short or long and lists vowel assimilations. 'Stress' appears twice, and both times it is a grammatically conditioned prominence used to tell tenses apart: in the -aho- past tense the 3sg prefix a (underlying aa) 'has a stress', whereas in the preceding tense the -ho- syllable is emphasized (p. 290); in the Past Conditional (-a- + -ale/-ele/-ile) the first syllable (the prefix vowel a, marked with an acute) is stressed to distinguish it from the relative form (p. 292). These are contrasts on specific morphemes, not a rule for the word.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only remarks are the two tense-specific contrasts quoted
new_statements.identity_note: Woodward 1926 describes the Makua of the Ruvuma district (UMCA Masasi mission field, Tanzania; 'the country.. on the Ruvuma, both above and below the Lujenda'), a revision of Maples 1879 from the same area; this is the Tanzanian Meetto/Kimakua zone = makh1261 and not the coastal Mozambican varieties (Woodward notes that the Maugham booklet 'is no help to one studying the language in the Ruvuma district'). The catalog's Kisseberth 2003 record draws on the Ikorovere (Tunduru) and Imitthupi (Masasi) dialects of the same region. Ismail 2000 (unopened) is titled for the 'Meto variety'.

tone_statements.citation: Cassimjee, Farida & Charles W. Kisseberth. 1999. A conspiracy argument for Optimality Theory: Emakhuwa dialectology. University of Pennsylvania Working Papers in Linguistics 6(1): 81-96.
tone_statements.quote: We have studied the tonal system of over twenty dialects of Emakhuwa, but will be restricting ourselves in this paper to three: Ikorovere, Eerati, and Esaaka. Moras in underlying representations in Emakhuwa may be either High- toned or not. [...] In all varieties of Emakhuwa known to us, there are no lexical tone contrasts in verb stems. The distribution of High versus toneless moras is determined by the moraic structure of the verb stem and the morphology in which it is embedded. Furthermore, lexical tone contrasts in nominal and other stems are extremely marginal in most Emakhuwa dialects.

tone_statements.quote: The most fundamental principle of Makua … tonology is a rule that we will refer to as HIGH TONE DOUBLING (HTD). It says simply that if a tone-bearing unit (TBU) has a high tone associated with it, then that high tone will also associate with the immediately following TBU. … In Ikorovere, both the basic high tone and also the doubled high tone are consistently pronounced as level high tones … All prefixes that consist phonetically of a single nasal consonant are tone-bearing--i.e. they may either have a high tone or a low tone associated with them.

tone_statements.summary: High vs low on tone-bearing units (vowel morae, some nasals); each high doubles onto the next unit, blocked phrase-finally; in Imithupi some highs surface mid or slightly falling; nothing on stress.

sources.note: Emakhuwa moras are underlyingly H or toneless; no lexical tone contrast in verb stems in any variety known to the authors, nominal lexical tone 'extremely marginal'; H placement is morphological (e.g. V1-V3 pattern in the infinitive); some varieties realise H in situ (no tone rules), others have High Tone Doubling (Ikorovere, Eerati: general doubling blocked onto an IP-final mora and onto the second mora of an IP-penult bimoraic syllable; Esaaka: doubling only in a restricted context) -- used as a conspiracy argument for OT (Optimal Domains).

sources.note: Makua (Ikorovere and Imithupi dialects, Tanzania) is analysed autosegmentally with a primary High (lexically idiosyncratic on nouns/formatives or assigned by morphologically triggered rule; 'verbal stems do not have lexical tone') that doubles onto the next tone-bearing unit (High Tone Doubling), with Phrase-Final Lowering and Long Fall deleting the doubled H, plus Short Fall and a Mid-Tone rule in Imithupi. The tone-bearing unit is the vowel (mora), not the syllable, and pre-consonantal nasals derived from NV are always tone-bearing while other pre-consonantal nasals must be lexically marked…
